events.speaker: facilitator
events.text:
"Transubstantiation" is a word and a way of thinking that comes later than Chloe's time - it gets worked out formally in the thirteenth century. So it's not something Chloe's world had a stake in, one way or the other.

For those unfamiliar: many Christians today use the term for the belief that in Communion, the bread and wine become, in their inner reality, the body and blood of Christ - while still looking and tasting like bread and wine. That's simply a description of the idea. Whether it's true, or whether Chloe's world would have leaned toward it or away from it, isn't for me to say, and different Christian traditions today still disagree about it.

What I'll do instead is ask Chloe what her own world held about the bread and cup of that shared meal - in whatever terms her world actually used. If there was nothing quite like this question there, she'll say so.

events.speaker: chloe
events.text:
We give thanks over the bread and the cup. That much stands everywhere among us. What we say varies more than a settled people might expect.

In the households formed by the Didache's own order, the thanksgiving is not for a body and blood given, but for the vine of David made known through Jesus, and for life and knowledge made known through him. The bread's own meaning there is gathering — scattered grain brought into one loaf, the way we ask that the church be gathered from the ends of the earth into the kingdom. No supper is told. No betrayal, no night handed over. Just thanksgiving, and the plea that we be made one as the loaf was made one.

In other households — Justin's own household is the fullest account that has reached us — the bread and the cup are not common food. He tells us plainly that we do not receive them as ordinary bread and ordinary drink, but as the flesh and blood of the one made flesh, through a word of prayer that comes from him. That is a different center entirely from the Didache's own thanksgiving for the vine.

We have not settled this into one teaching. Ignatius, writing under guard, presses hard that there be one altar and one eucharist under the bishop — but even he is arguing for unity of table, not laying out one settled account of what the bread and cup are. What we hold in common is thanksgiving itself, and the table as the place we are re-formed into one body. What each household says that bread and cup *are*, beyond that — we have genuinely different words for it, and I will not pretend to you that they have been made to agree.

citations.key_sources:
Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8 (agape requiring the bishop — ἀγάπην ποιεῖν in the Greek; verified against the Roberts-Donaldson/ANF translation). Pliny, Letters 10.96 (the separate, second-meal description this label is also proposed for, using no equivalent term at all — remains a source for the still-open cross-identification question).

Note: an earlier draft of this entry cited only Pliny and stated that the "agape" label was not primary-source-anchored — this was incorrect. Ignatius's own letter, already cited elsewhere in this world's lexicon for a different clause in the same chapter, uses this exact term for a real communal practice. This entry has been corrected accordingly.

Didache 9–10, 14 (thanksgiving prayers over cup and bread, no institution narrative). Ignatius, Letter to the Philadelphians 4 (the "one eucharist" instruction) and Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8 (bishop-validated eucharist — a related but separate instruction; Smyrnaeans 8 does not itself contain the "one eucharist" phrase). Justin Martyr, First Apology 65–67 (fullest surviving account — distribution to the absent, explanatory theology of the elements).

Note: Justin's account, despite being the fullest, should not be read as more representative simply because it is more explained — a live methodological caution this world's own reconstruction carries throughout rather than resolves. See CT Contest Type below.

Ignatius of Antioch, all seven letters (ekklesia as address and identity). 1 Clement (Rome to Corinth — ekklesia addressing ekklesia). Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians (ekklesia self-reference). Didache 4:14, 9–10, 14 (the gathering). Justin Martyr, First Apology 67 (the Sunday gathering described — cited here as a topical parallel; not part of this term's original evidentiary citation set).
See Source Identification below — Didache chs. 9–10, 14 (Registry P01).
